paragraphs.text: This tea comes from [Anhua](anhua:where-it-is), a mountain county on the middle Zi river, at the northern foot of the Xuefeng mountains in Hunan's Yiyang. It is hill and valley country where rice is hard to grow and tea does well. The county is warm and very wet, and the same air that grows the leaf is the air it is piled, pressed and kept in. That is why the trade ties the finished tea to [the place](anhua:why-people-value-it) and not only to the method.

Like all [dark tea](dark:definition), it was left to change in warmth and moisture after the leaf was made, so the trade calls it post-fermented. [Anhua dark tea](anhua-dark:definition) is a protected origin name in China, and every kind of it begins as one raw tea, [heimaocha](anhua-dark:making). That raw tea is made from large local leaf that is fixed, rolled, piled, rolled again and dried, then steamed soft and pressed.

This one dates from 2006 and has had twenty years. Anhua tea is kept for years and is said to [improve with keeping](anhua-dark:ageing), though no agreed number of years marks it as aged. Because of that, clean, dry and aired storage counts for as much as the time.

brewing.text: From a brick, cake or basket, ease the leaf off along the edge or from the top with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole pieces give up their flavour steadily; crumbs release it all at once and cloud the cup. In a small pot or gaiwan, use water at the boil and start with a steep of about 15 to 30 seconds, a little longer each round. Pressed and aged Anhua tea is also commonly simmered in a pot.

notice.text: A redder liquor, a sweeter, mellower cup, and sometimes a medicinal or herbal note.
